speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON PURCHASE OF WHEAT BY MEMBER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during recent weeks the government has been giving close study to the food situation in Colombo plan countries. Because of short crops on the Indian subcontinent, India and Pakistan have had to import unusually large quantities of wheat, much of it from the United States under the provisions of public law 480, in addition to their usual commercial purchases from traditional suppliers like Australia; and Ceylon will require additional food as a result of recent disastrous floods.
A few months ago, as the situation worsened, a decision was made to supply a limited quantity of wheat to both India and Pakistan and some flour to Ceylon out of available Colombo plan funds. This decision was warmly welcomed by these commonwealth countries. The totals could not be as large as we might have wished, $7 million to India, $2 million to Pakistan and $1 million to Ceylon, because the funds had already been largely committed for urgent purposes of national development.
Some weeks ago, the Indian government approached us to ascertain whether Canada would be prepared to supply additional wheat for payment over an extended period. Having in mind the great interest the Canadian people have shown in assisting India in its gigantic task of economic development, the government believed that parliament would wish to go as far as possible to meet the Indian request.
Accordingly negotiations have proceeded, and I am in a position to inform the house that an agreement has been reached between the Canadian wheat board and the Indian government for the supply of a quantity of 400,000 tons of wheat, approximately 15 million bushels, to be shipped during the winter
and early spring months. This agreement is subject to the conclusion of financial arrangements between the two governments which will provide, in brief, that payment will be made in seven equal annual instalments beginning three years after shipment. Interest is payable annually at a rate equal to the borrowing cost to the Canadian government plus a small charge for overhead. This rate is not likely to exceed 4J per cent.
These terms are, of course, most unusual. They are not terms that could be offered in ordinary commercial markets without the danger of turning cash sales into long-term credit sales. They can only be justified as part of Canada's effort to consolidate the very real gains that are being made in India, Pakistan and Ceylon and other Colombo plan countries, to prevent the serious setback which could result from the need to import and pay immediately for large scale imports of foods.
When the government of Pakistan was informed of these discussions with India they asked if wheat would be available to them on the same terms, and we assured them that the same terms would be available to all countries in receipt of assistance under the Colombo plan. Pakistan also requested that part of next year's Colombo plan appropriation be used for wheat. Because of prior commitments with respect to continuing projects this would have been difficult. But, as I shall indicate shortly, the government is proposing an increase which will be of assistance to Pakistan.
We have reason to believe that India will require additional quantities of wheat, over and above 400,000 tons, from Canada during the coming months. Some of this they may be prepared to buy on terms similar to those I have outlined. Pakistan and Ceylon and other countries within the Colombo plan may also make similar requests in due course.
The government is confident that parliament will support the provision of wheat and flour to Colombo plan countries on the terms I have outlined. We are also confident that at this difficult time in the affairs of our friends in south and southeast Asia, parliament and the people of Canada would wish to see an increase in the amount of aid in the form of outright grants that is being made available to them.
When the Minister of Finance brings down further supplementary estimates later this
2980	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry month parliament will be asked to vote approximately $30 or $35 million to be loaned to Colombo plan countries for the purchase of Canadian wheat and flour, and an additional $15 million as an outright grant for the same purpose. We have in mind that a part of the $15 million grant will be used to meet an urgent request for assistance by the government of Ceylon arising from the vhry serious floods that have caused such devastation in that country.
Canada has assumed responsibility to assist in the development of the countries of south and southeast Asia through the Colombo plan. This development is threatened by grave shortages of food. It is fortunate that our abundance coincides with their need and that we are in a position to play some further part in keeping this great effort of the free world moving ahead.
I am making this statement now so that plans for the movement of the wheat can proceed with a minimum of delay, and so that hon. members will be aware of this important development in government policy before they are asked to consider the relevant items in the estimates.

STARRED QUESTIONS
speechtext:
1.	On what date did the government of New Brunswick first request financial aid for Beech-wood from the present government of Canada?
2.	What was the form of the request and what was the nature and scale of the assistance requested?
3.	On what date did the government of Saskatchewan first request the present government to join with Saskatchewan in the South Saskatchewan project?
4.	On what date did the government of British Columbia approach the present government regarding the development of the Columbia river?
5.	Has any other provincial government made any request for assistance or co-operation In any power project?
6.	If so, which provincial governments and in respect of what projects?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: STARRED QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to parts 1 and 2 is that in a letter to the Prime Minister dated July 23, 1957, the premier of New Brunswick, Hon. Hugh John Flemming, said:
Federal assistance to the hydro development at Beechwood represents the most immediately required extension of the principle (of special assistance for the maritime area) in so far as New Brunswick is concerned.
A copy of this letter was tabled on January 3, 1958.
3.	The premier of Saskatchewan wrote to the Prime Minister on August 8 and in his letter he said:
Since your views and those of your party are well known on the desirability of the South Saskatchewan dam project, there is no need for me to stress the urgency for proceeding with it. However, it would be useful in preparing our budget if we knew when this undertaking was likely to be started and what contribution, if any, the Saskatchewan government would be expected to make over the next few years.
4.	This government has not been approached by the government of British Columbia regarding assistance in the development of the Columbia river.
With respect to parts 5 and 6, the government of Nova Scotia has requested assistance in respect of several projects coming within the scope of the Atlantic provinces program already announced for which the parliament will be asked to appropriate funds, and the details will be explained at that time. The government of Prince Edward Island, by telegram dated January 7, made clear its desire to have this Atlantic provinces program cover the provision of additional facilities to provide power to the island; the government of Newfoundland has also expressed its desire to have the program extend to that province. Assistance in regard to specific projects has not been requested by these governments.

NEWFOUNDLAND RAILWAY
speechtext:
1.	Is the government or the Canadian National Railways giving consideration to changing the gauge of the Newfoundland railway to standard gauge?
2.	If not, is it proposed to give consideration to such a change?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: NEWFOUNDLAND RAILWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I might deal with both parts of this question at the same time. Consideration is not being given to changing the gauge of the Newfoundland railway. I would point out that this matter has been raised on one or two occasions in the sittings of the sessional committee on railways and shipping, and I find that during the proceedings of this committee on March 18, 1957, the president of the Canadian National Railways stated as follows:
There is a very wrong impression that a narrow gauge railway is by definition an inefficient railway. That is not so. A narrow gauge railway can be just as efficient, if not more. In the peculiar circumstances of Newfoundland, and the peculiar circumstances under which your railway was built, in the matter of grades, curvatures, etc., a narrow gauge is a more efficient railway than a standard gauge would be. That is why I have said before, if the proposal were to build a standard gauge, we would never build a standard gauge on the same right of way as the narrow gauge is on. You would get a different idea about curvature, gradings, and everything else.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: FREIGHT RATES
subtopic: STATEMENT ON PROGRESS OF FREIGHT RATE EQUALIZATION INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon.
member for Assiniboia asked me a question regarding when it might be expected that the inquiry into the equalization of freight rates might be completed.
The board of transport commissioners has advised me as follows. The inquiry into the equalization of freight rates cannot be completed within a few months. The complicated freight rate structure of Canada includes millions of freight rates, and when the matter of equalization was before the parliamentary committee dealing with the proposed legislation, implementing recommendations of the Turgeon royal commission on transportation in 1951, evidence was given that it would take approximately five years to complete equalization. That estimate was in fact too low.
The board has proceeded to deal with the task of equalization as rapidly as possible, but since 1951 it has had a very heavy volume of work including a series of applications by the railways for freight rate increases.
The task of equalizing the "class" or maximum rates was accomplished and put

into effect on March 1, 1955, and the board then proceeded to deal with the lower rates on various bulk commodities, some of which have been dealt with to a conclusion. The board issued an extensive judgment in respect of these commodities in September last, and is proceeding with further hearings as expeditiously as possible. It has set down for hearing at Vancouver on March 3 next the equalization of rates on fruits, vegetables and lumber and a further hearing at Kelowna on March 10, and hearings at Calgary and Regina later in March respecting rates on coal.
In addition, the board has ordered the railways to submit equalized scales on cement, pulpwood, wood pulp and paper articles on or before March 31. Seventy-eight other scales have been ordered for revision on or before June 30. There are, however, many more rates to be dealt with.
The board submitted an interim report on equalization to his excellency the governor general in council in March, 1955, and a further report dated September 23, 1957. These reports gave details of the board's activities in connection with equalization of freight rates and indicated what progress had been made.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES
subtopic: STATEMENT ON PROGRESS OF FREIGHT RATE EQUALIZATION INQUIRY

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Timmins asked the Postmaster General the following question which bounced off to me:
Is the minister aware that the postal department has been involved in the infringement of two municipal by-laws in Burlington, Ontario, in regard to rented premises, as to which it is reported charges are to be laid? If so, is he in a position now to give the house any details on this matter?
The answer is that the Department of Public Works in providing a total of 2,025 square feet of temporary basement rented space for the Post Office Department located at 208 and 210 Brant street in Burlington, Ontario. Leases have not been signed as yet, but departmental approval has been given.
To date there is no correspondence on record to the effect that charges are to be laid against the crown for the infringement of two municipal by-laws in Burlington. However, the district architect's office advised by telephone this morning that (a) the owners have infringed on the municipal by-laws to the effect that they neglected to take out a building permit when altering the premises for occupancy; (b) neglected at that time to instal an emergency exit to satisfy the fire regulations as laid down by the municipal by-laws. This is reported to have been done now to the satisfaction of all concerned.
It will be seen from the above that if there is any infringement of city by-laws, it is by the owner of the building and not by the department.

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Finance to make loans, out of the consolidated revenue fund, to the government of New Brunswick, not exceeding thirty million dollars, in respect of expenditures for the development of hydro-electric power at Beechwood on the St. John river.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOAN OF $30 MILLION TO PROVINCE OF NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the bill to be founded on this resolution will authorize the government to make a loan to the government of New Brunswick in an amount not exceeding $30 million to cover the cost of constructing the Beechwood hydroelectric development on the St. John river.
May I remind the house that this resolution deals with a particular matter, that of assisting the province of New Brunswick in financing a specific and a very important project. There is another resolution on the order paper which my colleague the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will be introducing very shortly-indeed, it is the next item of business following the present resolution-which deals with the broader questions of the generation of electrical energy in the Atlantic provinces. May I express the hope that in this debate hon. members will address their attention to this Beechwood financing problem and if I may so request, reserve their views on the more general power problems of the Atlantic provinces until the other resolution and bill are before us.
The development of the power potential of the St. John river is not a new idea. As far back as 1910 the international joint commission undertook certain studies of its potential power resources, and a hydro-electric plant was built at Grand Falls shortly after the first world war. This power plant is privately owned. In line with the policy adopted by other provinces, the government of New Brunswick has for many years followed the policy of developing electrical energy by public ownership through the New Brunswick electric power commission.
Some nine years ago, that is early in 1949, the then premier of New Brunswick, foreseeing the growing need for expanded sources of energy, asked the federal government to invite the United States to join with it in requesting the international joint commission to make more detailed studies of the St. John river basin. In due course this work was

I am going to quote from these sessional papers, which will prove that the previous government never received the kind of request from the government of New Brunswick for assistance in respect to Beechwood with the conditions outlined by the Prime Minister the other day and by the Minister of Finance today.
On April 27, 1953, the government of New Brunswick presented to the government of Canada a brief on the need for financial assistance to develop the hydroelectric power resources of the St. John river. The request
Beechwood Power Project Loan of the government of New Brunswick was outlined on pages 5 and 6 of the brief as follows:
That the federal government advance to the province of New Brunswick the cost of developing the Beechwood hydroelectric power generating station, with projects incidental thereto. Estimated cost to 1960, $44,400,000.
Which is much more than $30 million.
That the funds be interest free or, if this should prove to be impossible, that the interest rate be 2\ per cent and interest free during construction.
And finally:
That repayments be made at the rate of 1.5 per cent of the principal amount each year,-
That is a 66-year period, not an 8-year period.
-the first payment to be due one year after the completion of the particular project for which the money was advanced.
The government of New Brunswick then projected the following development for Beechwood, and I will quote from page 3 of the brief:
The initial installation at Beechwood would be two 45,000 H.P. units, which is feasible on a run of river basis. The second step would be the development of 600,000 acre feet of storage in the upper reaches of the river. The completion of this storage development would be followed by the installation of a third unit at Beechwood together with the necessary transmission facilities.
The estimate of the cost of the two first units was at that time $24,200,000. Between 1953 and 1955 the program of the government of New Brunswick was amended, substantially changed, and in January, 1956, the government of New Brunswick presented a new brief to the government of Canada on the need for federal financial assistance for the development of electric power. The proposals of the New Brunswick government can be found on pages 16 and 17 of the brief, and I quote:
The government of New Brunswick urges that the government of Canada assist it in developing the electric generating capacity which will be required for a rapidly expanding New Brunswick economy. It requests the federal government to consider the following alternative proposals:
(1) The government of Canada to advance to the government of New Brunswick the necessary capital for the development of the hydro power of the St. John river basin. The rate of interest to be that prevailing on long term government of Canada bonds. Funds to be advanced for each project as they are required for the load of the New Brunswick electric power commission, and as it proves to be economically feasible as compared with alternative sources of power.
The estimate of the funds which would be required up to March 31,	1967, is

The alternative to that proposal was the following:
The government of Canada to advance to the government of New Brunswick the funds required

Beechwood Power Project Loan for the projected construction program of the New Brunswick electric power commission through to March 31, 1967, the rate of interest to he that prevailing on long term government of Canada bonds. Funds required are estimated at $211,094,000.
In the second brief there was no direct proposal as to the annual rate of capital reimbursement, but the rate of depreciation was the same as in the first brief, 1.5 per cent a year over a period of 66 years.

After all, if we are to be fair all around with our provinces and with the money that properly belongs to the people of Canada, we must know that when advances are to be made out of the consolidated revenue fund the proposition is sound, and there is a good chance that the province to which the loan is made will be able to pay it back.
I have listed a number of questions which were asked by the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet, and I will repeat them and ask the ministers concerned, before the second reading of the bill, to give us answers to these questions. In the first place, let me assure the minister and the committee that we believe that at times it is necessary for the federal treasury to come to the assistance of provinces in order to ensure the proper development of the resources of those provinces. We do know that the province of New Brunswick has had a depressed economy for some years; that has been quite clear. They have required help, and there is no doubt about that. We have been, in our group, sympathetic to whatever help could be granted to New Brunswick so they could get a proper development; because we realize that unless they have power down there, and sufficient power, they cannot proceed to industrialize to any degree.
One of the things they need above all others is industry in order to ensure employment for their people and the fullest measure of development of their resources. I am going back a little in the history of power development in New Brunswick. A major part of the electric power development in New Brunswick has taken place within my memory; in fact in my own home town of St. Andrews we have only enjoyed this necessary service since 1920. In that year a little company composed of citizens of that town was formed, electrical energy was purchased from the Canadian Pacific Railway through their facilities at the Algonquin hotel. It was steam-generated power. We paid for that service in the little town from which I come at 16 cents per kilowatt hour plus a $1 a month service charge. We also found it necessary to pay for the meter that measured the energy.
That was my first experience with the cost of electrical energy in the province of New Brunswick. After two or three years it was determined that some cheaper source of power must be found, and for a few years we were serviced from the Canadian Cotton Mills in Milltown. That power was sent over the St. Croix river by an underwater cable to St. Andrews and we were serviced in that way. Later on it was taken over by the New Brunswick power commission.

Beechwood Power Project Loan
The first development we enjoyed in New Brunswick in so far as water power is concerned took place at Musquash in Saint John county. That was a very successful development. It has been in operation, I would say, for 27 or 28 years. It has been a great convenience and has meant a great deal to the people of the province of New Brunswick. That project was sponsored and built by a Liberal government for this purpose. They wanted to be able to provide electrical energy for the citizens of our province at cost. As I have pointed out, prior to that time the cost of electrical energy in that province was prohibitive. There were many appliances we wished to have in our homes but which we just could not have on account of the cost of energy.
That same government, namely the Liberal government, went ahead with plans for a much larger development at Grand Falls, which is well known to the Liberal members of this house here. There is no doubt in my mind that Grand Falls was the greatest water development in the maritime provinces. Arrangements and agreements had been completed with the province of Quebec and the state of Maine for storage facilities away back in 1925. Baxter formed a Tory government in our province. What happened? He immediately withdrew those tenders that had been called, and sold our birthright at Grand Falls to the Gatineau Power Company.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking before one o'clock there were two statements I made which were, I know, believed to be incorrect by two hon. members sitting on the other side of the house. I referred to the New Brunswick hydroelectric power commission taking over the electrical system in Saint John city. I have checked since I left the chamber at one o'clock, and I find that the New Brunswick electric power
Beechwood Power Project Loan commission did take over what is known as the New Brunswick power company, the producing company in Saint John, and today only that producing company distributes power. It is owned and controlled by the New Brunswick electrical power commission.
I also stated that between 1930 and 1935 no improvements had been made in the way of power development in New Brunswick. I find that during that period one plant was built at Minto, New Brunswick in 1933, and I also find that the highest cost power produced in New Brunswick comes from that plant. The latest figure I have is 22 mills.
I stated earlier today that those who sit on this side of the house and who come from New Brunswick have always maintained and still maintain that Beechwood would never provide a stable source of power until storage rights had been secured. This stand that has been taken over the years was based on information which we were able to obtain from those who were qualified to give it. I know the former premier of New Brunswick was very very much convinced that storage rights were necessary. One of the main sources of information we have had in New Brunswick was the late Gaspard Boucher, who was at one time chairman of the hydro company. He gave me these same views; and in order that there may be no misunderstanding I should like to put on the record a statement made in the budget debate in the provincial legislature at Fredericton in 1952, just previous to the provincial election of that year. In speaking in that debate Hon. J. B. McNair had this to say:
It was upwards of six years ago that fresh studies were launched to determine the power potential of the Saint John river. These were initiated through the New Brunswick resources development board. As a result of its work we early became convinced that, in addition to others the merits of which have long been considered debateable, there are two potential sites capable of economic development. These are the sites at Morrill and just above Beechwood enumerated in this house by my friend opposite a few weeks ago.
Our studies have been predicated upon the assumption that storage is vital to any development. We know too. as he said in his speech, that sections of the river constituting boundary waters as well as tributaries, outside this province would be involved. We have also been aware that heavy expenditures would be involved in any development program.
It seemed to us necessary to enlist interest and support elsewhere if any plans were to be developed for the effective harnessing of the power of the Saint John river system.
. . . On December 8, 1948, I wrote the Prime Minister of Canada requesting the co-operation of the Canadian government and that steps be taken to refer to the international joint commission the study of the power potential of the Saint John

Beechwood Power Project Loan river system and means to make it effective. I feel it desirable that this letter should also be read into the records of this house. It is as follows:
Then here is the letter sent by Hon. J. B. McNair to the Prime Minister of Canada at that time.
In New Brunswick as elsewhere in Canada the demand for electric energy is increasing at an unprecedented rate. For some years efforts have been made by our publicly owned electric power commission to meet the needs in this province by additions to its coal steam generating system and in certain areas by the temporary and costly expedient of installing diesel units to meet pressing local shortages of supply. During the past few years certain surveys and studies of sites where hydro-electric energy might be economically produced, have been carried on. In these we have had the assistance of such engineering firms of the Power Corporation of Canada and H. G. Acres and Company.
During these investigations consideration has been given to further hydro-electna development on the Saint John river, the largest of the rivers of the maritime provinces. As you may know, about 20 years ago a hydro-electric plant was established at Grand Falls which is presently owned and operated by the Gatineau Power Company. Apart from this there are other sites, possibly three, farther down the river which may lend themselves to development. One of them is now receiving intensive study and appears very promising. However, any such development is rendered problematical due to lack of storage and regulation of flow, factors very material to steady energy production throughout the year.
The history of the Grand Falls plant, which primarily supplies the newsprint mill of the International Paper Company at Dalhousie, has shown a drop during the winter season from its designed and installed capacity of 80,000 H.P. to an output of 20,000 H.P. or less. Any new installation on the river would be subject to similar winter and late summer or early autumn fluctuations in production.
The solution of this problem lies in the provision of storage in the headwaters of the Saint John river. These lie chiefly in the state of Maine and in the province of Quebec. Available statistics show that the drainage area of the Saint John river above Grand Falls is about equally divided between Maine and Quebec with approximately 4,500 square miles in each jurisdiction.
It was of interest to us to note that the newly reorganized international joint commission is now giving study to various boundary water questions. It would seem that the time is opportune to seek its assistance and intervention in connection with the hydro-electric potential of the Saint John river. It is obvious that apart from other possibilities there is storage of considerable magnitude available on the St. Francis river, one of its tributaries. This river rises in Quebec and for a portion of its course forms the boundary between Maine and Quebec and then becomes the boundary between Maine and New Brunswick. In these boundary waters are to be found three lakes known as Glasier, Cross and Beau lakes which constitute wide stretches in the river which should lend themselves to storage works and if developed would afford most helpful storage during periods of low water supply for any present or future development on the Saint John river. It clearly falls within the jurisdiction of the international joint commission.
In every part of that speech made in the budget debate by Hon. John B. McNair he
[Mr. Stuart (Charlottel-1
outlined in every detail the absolute necessity of storage rights on the St. John river before stable power could ever be produced. That was the attitude that was taken 20 years ago, and it is the attitude that is taken today. Nevertheless it was decided by the provincial government of New Brunswick to go ahead with that project without storage rights.
To confirm the ideas that have been expressed by Liberal members of this house I should now like to put on the record a statement by one who is very closely connected with the New Brunswick power commission, Dr. Rowley. In his 1955 report which was published and put out by the provincial government of New Brunswick, Dr. Rowley, director of the research branch of the New Brunswick resources development board, had this to say:
Until large water storages are constructed In the upper reaches of the Saint John river watershed in Maine and Quebec, such firm or continuous power will not be available from sites that might be developed on the main river. With ample water flowing, as during the spring run-offs and with rainy autumn periods, Beechwood will afford periods of firmness in supply. The smaller winter and summer flows will afford energy for some hours each day only to care for peaks when system demand is high. Consequently new sources of continuous power must be afforded and these are most likely to be steam plants burning that fuel which will most effectively yield power at the lowest cost.
No stronger support could be given to the stand taken by Mr. J. B. McNair in New Brunswick than that statement by Dr. Rowley. I have been convinced for many years that Beechwood would never be economically sound, would never provide stable and dependable power, until those storage rights had been secured, and I believe that idea has today taken form in the minds of many people in New Brunswick. It is for that reason that on many occasions when I have spoken on this matter I have been accused of opposition for political reasons. But that would not greatly affect the people in my province, because they know that the whole issue has been shrouded in politics for years and years.
It was the belief of many people in New Brunswick that this development should never have been taken out of its international setting; that we should have gone ahead by obtaining those storage rights, and in that way we could have been supplied with dependable power from Beechwood. You must have dependable power before you can interest those who might come to the area and establish industries. You cannot attract industry when you have low power during one part of the year and high power at another period.

In rising to speak in support of this resolution, Mr. Chairman, I wish to express the gratitude of the people of my constituency for a measure which has been hailed not only in the constituency of York-Sunbury but throughout the whole province of New Brunswick. I have no doubt that when the speech from the throne was read by Her Majesty on October 14 and Beech-wood was mentioned, there were many people listening to whom Beechwood was only a name. There are those who think of Beechwood only as a hydroelectric development on the Saint John river 100 miles or so above the capital city of Fredericton, but Beechwood is a great deal more than that. Beechwood is a symbol, an example of the courageous determination of the people of New Brunswick to improve their lot, to improve their standard of living.
A few days ago I was reading a volume on our Atlantic provinces. The harsh first sentence in the chapter on my province was in these words:
New Brunswick is a poverty-stricken land which occasionally sprouts a millionaire.
Those are the words of the author, Mr. Chairman, not mine. New Brunswick was not always a poverty-stricken land. When New Brunswick joined with Nova Scotia and Upper and Lower Canada to form this great nation, it was anything but poverty-stricken. Its lumber was shipped all over the world. Saint John was the second largest shipbuilding port in the world. It traded heavily with the New England states, the West Indies and Europe. As the result of the federal union we lost the valuable United States trade, trade which was never regained.

Mr. Chairman, the resolution before us now has to do with a measure to authorize a loan out of the consolidated revenue fund to the government of New Brunswick, not exceeding $30 million, to cover the full cost of construction of the Beechwood plant. The terms of the loan have been outlined by the Minister of Finance this morning, and the loan is to bear interest of 4| per cent or the current rate of interest of long-term Canadian loans at the time the loan will be made on April 1, and is to be repayable in a period of eight years.
The Canadian people were first informed of the government's decision in this connection when in the speech from the throne the following words were spoken by Her Gracious Majesty the Queen:
You will also be asked to provide assistance in financing the Beechwood project which has been under construction in New Brunswick.

speechtext:
In a statement issued to the press two days later Premier Hugh John Flemming said:
It has been a moving experience to represent New Brunswick in Ottawa during the opening of parliament by Her Majesty, and to hear set forth in the speech from the throne the promise of Her Majesty's government of Canada to assist the Beechwood development and to make further provision for the generation of lower cost power in the Atlantic area.
Further on he makes reference to this generous promise in the speech from the throne, and concludes his statement by saying:
Altogether, the speech from the throne contained news of great and hopeful significance for every man, woman and child in this province.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that on the government side of the house there is some confusion about the present status of the Beechwood project. This morning, in an interjection, the Minister of Veterans Affairs said that Beechwood had been in operation for three weeks. Amongst the sessional papers which were tabled on January 3 there is a letter dated October 21, 1957 from the Prime Minister of Canada to Hon. Hugh John Flemming, premier of New Brunswick. This letter reads as follows:
My dear Premier:
I wish to send you my congratulations and best wishes on the occasion of the formal opening of the Beechwood hydro development project next Thursday, October 24.
Now, whom are we to believe? This is in a sessional paper which was produced on January 3, amongst all those letters of congratulations from the Prime Minister and other ministers of the cabinet; but the real document which was requested, the proposal of the federal government to the province of New Brunswick, was not tabled.
It is my intention this afternoon to review briefly some of the incidents and discussions relating to federal assistance to electric power development in New Brunswick, leading to this so-called generous reference of such hopeful significance. The interim report of the international joint commission of the United States and Canada on the water resources of the Saint John river basin involving Quebec, Maine and New Brunswick, released on January 27, 1954, included, in conjunction with the Beechwood project on the Saint John river, provision for a 500,000 to 600,000 acre feet reserve storage at sites upstream from Grand Falls, New Brunswick. This would have made possible the prospective increase in normal power demand through 1961, with thermal plants to meet the requirements of extraordinary demands such as may be required by mineral developments in northern New Brunswick. We all

recognize that thermal expansion would be less economical than storage; nevertheless it appears to be the only alternative if storage is not made available in order to increase the total output of the present Beechwood installation by the addition of a third 45,000 horsepower unit, or even to assure the potential electrical output of the present units.
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I may refer to the words of the premier of New Brunswick himself when addressing the New Brunswick legislative assembly on April 14, 1954. He said, and I quote his own words:
All this information has gone to show that the outstanding question in regard to power development is the amount of financial assistance which could be secured by the province in developing the Saint John river. It has already been announced by the hon. chairman-
That is the chairman of the New Brunswick hydro commission.
-that the province, on its own behalf, can and will begin the initial development at Beechwood. However, the great storage projects will require assistance when they are undertaken-assistance which can only come from one source.
In view of these words by the premier of New Brunswick himself I am wondering how the members on the government side can protest the attitude of the previous government on this matter.
We should deduce from this statement by the premier of New Brunswick that the province, on its own behalf, could proceed and decided to proceed with the initial development of Beechwood. The premier stated at the time, and this was less than four years ago, that where assistance was required and where it was expected was for the acquisition and construction of the great storage projects which were needed in order to make the Beechwood operation effective and economical.
In view of this statement by the premier of New Brunswick, and in view of the decision, according to this statement, to proceed with the initial stage of the Beechwood project, which in fact has been now practically completed and is in operation, it is clear that the previous federal government had taken very important decisions concerning this vital question. On January 26, 1956, as reported on page 558 of Hansard for that date, I received a reply from the then minister of northern affairs and national resources which reads in part as follows:
AH the way along there has been a constant exchange of views among provincial and federal technical and financial officials. These discussions appeared to indicate that the development to the end of the Beechwood phase could be carried out by the province of New Brunswick without jeopardizing its credit. It appears, however, that future developments in the province are likely to require additional power on a substantial scale.

This larger future development has been represented to the federal government as likely to be beyond the capacity of the province of New Brunswick to finance on its own.
The previous government was prepared to recognize that the larger future development of the Saint John river was beyond the capacity of New Brunswick to finance on its own, and also to take into consideration the admission by the premier of New Brunswick himself that the present phase of the project, the one which we are discussing today, could be undertaken by the province on its own.
In his budget presentation on March 14 last the former minister of finance outlined a proposal which was offered to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and which has been referred to by those who have preceded me in this debate. In concluding his remarks the minister stated that notwithstanding his offer, the relatively high cost of electrical power in the Atlantic region as a whole would continue to receive further careful study.
The latest available report on this important subject is the report on the power supply of New Brunswick and Nova Seotia, made for the Northern Canada Power Commission by the Montreal Engineering Company Limited, which was finally tabled in this house a few weeks ago by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. On page 8 of this report we find this:
The two hydro units now being installed in the Beechwood plant, can be used to good advantage for supplying peak power and secondary energy. Unless storage is developed in the United States or Quebec, the water supply will be inadequate to justify the installation of a third unit in the period under review.
On this very subject of water storage, a day or two ago I came across a statement made by Mr. H. J. Rowley, director of the research board and chairman of the New Brunswick development board, which was included in his 1955 report to the department of industry and development of his province. I feel that this statement by Dr. Rowley, which was quoted in full a few minutes ago by my colleague the hon. member for Charlotte, has a direct bearing on the motion which is now under consideration by this committee. Here is a statement by an expert in this field. Here is a straightforward report which reveals without any doubt that water storage facilities are essential to the economic development or operation of the Beechwood project.
From the statements I have just placed on the record it is obvious that the government would have been well advised to advance money to provide water storage facilities which are essential to the economical operation of Beechwood, rather than share in
Beechwood Power Project Loan financing a project which is already completed and in fact partially in operation. If this is a general policy to be adopted by the government the minister should advise the house accordingly.
Personally I would have preferred to see the government advance money for the storage facilities, which would have contributed to making the Beechwood project not only economically sound but would at the same time have provided employment which is so urgently needed in New Brunswick today. In fact, had the province of New Brunswick financed the project in 1954, when the premier announced that the province could and would proceed on its own with the construction of Beechwood, when loans could be obtained at an interest rate of 3i per cent to 3f per cent, the ratepayers of the province of New Brunswick would have been saved from $250,000 to $300,000 a year in interest alone.
In making his announcement, on November 14 last, part of which I referred to earlier, the Prime Minister stated that the Beechwood plant would provide a substantial block of relatively low cost power. Has the minister today given any indication of the cost of this relatively low cost power for which a loan is asked? Has the Prime Minister, when he made his announcement on November 14 last, or the Minister of Finance when introducing the resolution we are now discussing, given any assurance to this house that relatively low cost power could be produced if this loan were approved?
In the same address to the provincial legislature which I mentioned earlier, on April 14, 1954, the premier of New Brunswick said:
The Conservative party has been the strongest advocate of the storage scheme during recent years.
If they are so strong an advocate of the storage scheme, why are they not asking for the co-operation of the federal government to take care of the 500,000 or 600,000 acre feet storage required to make Beechwood economically sound, and the only way to provide the relatively low cost power which New Brunswick industries are asking for? The construction of storage facilities at this time, when unemployment in New Brunswick has reached an all-time high, would provide work for a large number of our unemployed.
Where is today the news of great and hopeful significance for every man, woman and child in New Brunswick? Is it to be found in the recent curbing actions by the United States government or in the further restrictions which can be expected following the

Beechwood Power Project Loan bold and arrogant attitude of the present government? Is it to be found in the ever-increasing unemployment which is spreading through New Brunswick and through all Canada today?
The people of Bathurst and of Gloucester county have been seriously shocked by the recent announcement of the curtailment of operations by Brunswick Mining and Smelting Corporation. There is a possibility that lead and zinc are next on the list to be affected by United States import curtailment. Is it not significant that over six months after taking office the present government have not produced a single official note of protest, a single official document having to do with representations to the United States government, asking for postponement of such curbing actions toward imports from a neighbouring and friendly country? No one in New Brunswick, particularly in Gloucester county, can disregard the serious blow to our people and to our economy that will follow the curtailment of mining operations in the Bathurst area.
For the last four years our merchants, our industries and our people had geared and planned their activities on developments which had given new hopes to our depressed areas and which had promised a revolution in our general economy. Investments were made accordingly. New constructions were started, some of which are now completed. New accommodations were provided and Bathurst, conscious of its responsibility, was looking ahead to a future of achievement in material things, of progress in civic affairs, ready to take full advantage of its human resources as well as its new natural resources.
If the present government was prepared to take action to keep in operation the Britannia mines in British Columbia, and if the present government is consistent in its policy to help the Atlantic provinces, why is it not taking action to keep in operation the mining developments in northern New Brunswick? I will have more to say on this subject on resolution No. 11, having to do with assistance in the generation of electrical energy by thermal power projects for the Atlantic provinces.
When normal amortization periods on power plants built by the Northern Canada Power Commission are based on a long term amortization period of 30 years, why is the loan now granted to New Brunswick for the Beechwood project limited to an eight year repayment period? It is only logical to assume that the province of New Brunswick with its declining revenues mainly in the last few months, will not be in a position to repay this loan on the basis of $4 million per year.


In other words, if New Brunswick wants to meet its obligations under this particular loan it may have to borrow at a higher rate of interest. Before this bill is presented the minister should consider very seriously extending the amortization period to conform with the policy in regard to northern power development.
In concluding I wish to quote a brief paragraph from the Atlantic Advocate, a magazine from the maritime provinces which I am sure, through its editor and publisher, is well known to the members on the government side of the house. Before doing so, however, I want to take this opportunity to congratulate the Atlantic Advocate, which won high honour by receiving the annual award of the Canadian tourist association's historical and cultural committee. This, and the public references in speeches and newspapers that followed, have combined to make the first year-end of publishing a happy and rewarding climax. Under the title "Looking a Gift Horse in the Mouth" the editor of the Atlantic Advocate has the following words to say:
For it is a natural and proper reluctance that causes hesitancy to look a gift horse in the mouth. Ingratitude is one of the baser qualities. Yet, whilst we are glad to get acceptance of the principle of adjustment grants to poorer provinces, and grateful for the thermal units, the coal subsidy that goes with them, the grid, and the financing of Beechwood, we must admit to disappointment that the coal subsidy, limited as it is to $1,600,000, will not be sufficient to remove the differential between power prices in the Atlantic area and elsewhere: and the federal financing of Beechwood with interest at 4g per cent and repayment spread over eight years is not the low interest long term financing the province looked for.

In view of the fact that on two occasions the present hon. member for Cape Breton South has clearly indicated to this house that he would prefer to settle issues by fisticuffs outside of the house rather than by exhibiting his ability to debate issues inside the house, I suggest that he model his conduct on that of the former member for Cape Breton South who, I think I am safe in saying, had the respect of his colleagues in this house, whose ability was recognized by members of all parties, who on all occasions respected the highest and best traditions of parliamentary procedure, and who always aimed to achieve his ends in strictly Canadian and constitutional ways. In all kindness to the young member I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in order to become thoroughly housebroken to the days ahead he read very carefully the speeches his predecessor made from 1942 until the dissolution of parliament this year.
This group has remained silent on this resolution to date, Mr. Chairman, because it is quite content to sit here and glow with

pride and satisfaction in the knowledge that this government is following the procedure of the former Liberal government in adopting as policy some segments of C.C.F. policy that have been advocated in this house for many years.
In this resolution the present government is adopting the policy that has been urged by members of this group for many years; that is for a federal government to render financial assistance to a provincial government for the development of hydro resources under public ownership. We are very pleased to see this and we realize it is further evidence-and it happens from day to day- that even governments learn from this little and valiant group on this side of the house, that our policies are substantially sound and that we are effective out of all proportion to our numbers at the present time. I hope the people of Canada in general will recognize these facts at the next election.
I have taken a great deal of interest in the development of hydro resources and in deference to the expressed wishes of the Minister of Finance I am going to defer my remarks with respect to the validity of public ownership for the next resolution, because I do not want to stir him up at this time. I do want to put on record, however, the report which General McNaughton made to the external affairs committee with respect to the Saint John river development of which I understand the Beechwood development is an important part, because I think the member for Charlotte was rather critical of that development. I have the report given by General McNaughton to the external affairs committee, but there were certain questions asked and we do not have a printed copy of the record at this time. I propose now to read from the report on the Saint John river reference, 1950, as amended July 7, 1952, as I think this should be placed on the record:
Again in the maritimes, I would like to report briefly on the Saint John river reference. As I mentioned last year the interim report of the commission dated January 27, 1954 is in the hands of the governments and since that time, we have received annual reports from the engineering board covering subsequent developments in the area.
I am pleased to report that the first two units of New Brunswick's Beechwood power project are now in place and will be in operation shortly. Action is being taken to provide electrical interconnection between New Brunswick and Maine which was recommended in the commission's report. In this respect I recall that on my appearance before this committee last year I was able to report that the state of Maine had repealed the Fernald Act which had prohibited the export of hydro-electric power from that state. Action has since been taken b.y the Department of Trade and Commerce (Canada) and by the United States
Beechwood Power Project Loan
federal power commission to authorize the interconnection and the export of electric energy in the amounts proposed. The amounts are not large in comparison to various blocks of power available in other parts of Canada but under the special conditions of development in the region largely along the two sides of the Saint John river these arrangements should prove of material help in satisfying local needs of the area and we are hopeful that later these arrangements for cooperation may be further extended to the benefit of development in the Saint John river basin both in Canada and in the United States.
I judge from the report of the general and the answers to the questions of that committee that while this whole scheme of development has not come to fruition with respect to the arrangements between Canada and the United States-and to the hydro development this is a very important and worth-while step in this direction-we in this group give wholehearted support to this resolution as providing for a measure that will be of great advantage to the people and to the economy of the province of New Brunswick.

I would like to say a few words in support of this resolution. As a matter of fact I think I would be less than

Beechwood Power Project Loan human if I did not at this time, not only-express my own appreciation for the early recognition by the government of the necessity of helping a small province but also express the appreciation of the people of my constituency because this project happens to be in that constituency. Indeed I might go a step further and say that the people of New Brunswick in general appreciate the action taken by this government in such an early recognition of their needs.
I would like to be fair, but I cannot let pass some remarks made by hon. members today. I am wondering if they are trying to convince the members of this house that this resolution and the legislation which follows it should not be supported. Neither the hon. member for Charlotte nor the hon. member for Gloucester indicated that they were going to support the legislation and I wonder if they are going to do so. Even though it is not as good as they would like to see it, is it so bad that they are going to vote against it? I am sure they have not convinced the members of this house that this project is an unworthy one but I am afraid that the impression is going out from this house, through those members, that it is not an economic, sound or even the type of project which the federal authority should support in a small province like New Brunswick.
If that impression should go out I would feel sorry because I am sure it could do nothing but hurt, not only those members in their own constituencies and in their own provinces but it might give a wrong impression to the rest of Canada as to the outlook we have in New Brunswick. After all, we are pretty solid citizens down there and we do not tackle anything unless we have a pretty good idea that we can carry it out.
The Beechwood project is the largest development that has ever been undertaken by the New Brunswick hydro commission and it was undertaken only after months and months of study and research. I would like, as strongly as I can, to impress upon the members of this house that I think they will find if they will look into the records that the project about to be completed-or that part of it which includes the two units-has been approved by the power corporation, by H. G. Acres and Company Limited and by the chairman of the Canadian section of the international joint commission.
It has been approved, and the New Brunswick hydro commission was given the go ahead for that part of the project as a sound economic development. So all those arguments which strive to indicate that because we cannot at the moment secure the rights from the state of Maine and from

the province of Quebec and settle the great problem of flowage everyone should keep their hands off Beechwood do no good for New Brunswick and no good for Canada.
This present policy is, if I understand it correctly, one of the first steps of the new government in the development of a natural resources policy which this country has so far lacked. All through the negotiations which were carried out between the provinces and the federal authorities there has emerged now and again a very good reason why the federal government did not back the province, and this was because they had no national development policy on which they could justify their claims.
I should like to refer to a letter dated February 3, 1954 from the federal authorities to the comptroller general of the province of New Brunswick in which the deputy minister of finance told the comptroller general:
Confirming our telephone conversation we have, as you know, given long and careful consideration to your proposals regarding federal assistance to the government of New Brunswick in financing the development of hydroelectric power on the Saint John river. I am now directed by my minister to say that he has reviewed this matter with his colleagues, and the conclusion has been reached that it would not be right or proper for the federal government to provide funds by loan or otherwise for the development of natural resources along the lines you suggest.

I certainly do mark those last words, and I tell the hon. member that the people of New Brunswick have got those last words underlined. If I had wanted to play politics, or try to do anything funny, I would leave them out; that is what hon. members on the other side usually do.
If my hon. friends want to look up Hansard for a few years back they will find it recorded that the former minister of finance, Mr. Abbott, made a statement in this house while sitting on this side of the chamber that it was not the policy of the federal government to finance any project for a provincial authority which they should finance themselves and pay for over a period of years. In other words, that statement was right in line with this letter. There was no federal natural development policy available on the basis of which the government could see their way to giving assistance to a province. Therefore they did not do so. They never provided any assistance in this regard, either to New Brunswick or to any other province. The step which the government is now undertaking is a step toward the development of the type of policy which I believe will, as it unfolds, offer every province a chance when it has a proposition

which is sound economically, feasible of accomplishment and able to pay its way. That is exactly what we have in the Saint John river hydro development at Beechwood today.
This project was begun on June 11, 1955. Before proceeding further I will say that ever since that day the people concerned with the project in New Brunswick, both the federal authorities and the hydro authorities have tried to keep politics out of it. At no time, in my view, have they ever originated the idea of making this a political football. On the occasion of the opening ceremony the federal government was represented by the former minister of trade and commerce, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe. Also present was chairman of the Canadian section of the international joint commission, General McNaughton; officials of the hydro electric authority of the state of Maine, members of the government of the province of New Brunswick and, in addition, distinguished members and leaders of the opposition at that time, along with members of the New Brunswick power commission. All these people took part in this opening ceremony. It was not a political occasion.
Moreover, as I understand it, since 1953 when the new government came into power in New Brunswick the opposition in New Brunswick, which comprised the remnants of the Liberal party, supported this proposal; as far as I know they have never opposed it; it has been non political.
In addition to receiving the support of all these public men, this tremendous undertaking was brought into being at a time when the province was just recovering from a period of financial difficulties which had lasted for several years; I am referring to 1953 and 1954. And if ever a province needed assistance, New Brunswick needed it then. At that time the federal authorities gave encouragement to those in the province with whom they were in contact. They never refused to discuss this question, and that is borne out by all the correspondence which has been conducted between the authorities. The matter was on a basis of discussion, and I do not think any one can deny that discussions were carried on freely. I do not think anyone can deny that the federal authorities encouraged New Brunswick to proceed, as this was a solid project from the economic viewpoint.
However, the federal government always stopped short of saying, "We will back your bonds or supply money at a certain rate of interest," or something of that nature. It stopped short of the financial assistance which
Beechwood Power Project Loan was the final step needed to be taken to help us out. The lack of such backing would have discouraged many public men. Fortunately, however, a new government had recently been put in charge of our affairs in New Brunswick. It was a government of young businessmen who had faith in the future of New Brunswick and who tackled their work with vigour, confident that something could be done for New Brunswick. In addition to that they conveyed that feeling of enthusiasm to the people of the province as has been so ably demonstrated since that time. Thus it was that on June 11, 1955, when the first blast was set off, many thousands of people gathered at Beechwood to watch the opening.
What I am going to say now I say with all sincerity because I was present at that opening and spoke to many of the people who were gathered there. The people who spoke to me expected me to have the answer but I did not and of course the answer they were looking for did not come. The Right Hon. C. D. Howe was present on that occasion which was very encouraging to the people of New Brunswick when they gathered there that afternoon. When they saw the federal minister in attendance they were sure that before the meeting was over he was going to announce that the federal authority had decided to back the project but they went home disappointed. Perhaps they were not justified in their expectations but they did know that negotiations had been proceeding and many of them being supporters of the Liberal government were certain he would make the announcement because it was one of the first and biggest projects New Brunswick had undertaken that would benefit the province as a whole and would assist the future of our mining, lumbering, pulpwood and paper industries.
No announcement was made and so the New Brunswick hydro commission backed by the provincial government went ahead with the project. As you have heard today two units are now operating and the project has become an integral part of the support of our whole economic system, a necessity to the encouragement of mining expansion and the establishment of new industries. I am under the impression that General McNaughton advised the external affairs committee that there has already been a hookup with the hydro system of the state of Maine and this integration is of importance. Nevertheless the completion of this project by no means represents the fulfilment of our hydro development requirements in New Brunswick. I am not going to take time to labour the point because it is generally known and has already been stated by the hon. member for Charlotte that the cost of the development of power from the first thermal plant was extremely high and it

Beechwood Power Project Loan continues that way. In a province like New Brunswick or in any other small province that has very little potential hydroelectric development the cost of thermal electrical development is very expensive, but if you mix the two you can possibly arrive at the best average price. The greatest cost is the initial expenditure and there is the cost of repair and so on but ten years from now the cost may be quite different.
I do not think it is necessary to labour unduly the arguments in support of this resolution. I have been a member of this house for five years and during that time the question of hydro development in New Brunswick has often been discussed. In that period of time I have witnessed a significant change in the attitude of hon. members from other than the Atlantic provinces towards those of us who come from the maritimes. In 1955 and 1956 private members on all sides of the house were speaking on our behalf in an effort to impress on the federal government that the maritimes deserved assistance. Many hon. members who sat or who now sit in these benches came to me and discussed the question of hydro power in New Brunswick and were very sympathetic toward us. Some hon. members are not here today because they have passed on or have fallen by the wayside but their sympathetic attitude lingers after them and I believe the majority of hon. members of this committee today regardless of what province they come from are sympathetic toward us in the maritime provinces. They realize we are backward in our development in some respects and most of them are prepared to support us in trying to bring the standard of living in the Atlantic area in closer relationship to the standards enjoyed in other provinces.
Mention has been made today of the attitude held by some hon. members that the present interest rate is not going to provide cheap power. I do not think I am unfair when I say that if the previous federal government had adopted a policy under which it could have acted it could have backed the province of New Brunswick in 1954 and 1955 when these demands were made. It could have assisted the Beechwood development and financed it at an interest rate much less than the present 4| per cent. At that time the government could have arranged a loan at an interest rate more favourable than the rate under with the government must operate today. I do not think that we in New Brunswick expect the government to lend money to the province today at a cheaper rate of interest than that at which it can borrow but two years ago the federal authority was able to borrow

money at a cheaper rate than is possible today. If negotiations had been concluded and the federal government had come forward and offered a loan at cost plus administrative charges I am sure the interest rate would not have been more than 3i per cent and perhaps not that much and I feel sure that the province of New Brunswick would have gladly entered into an agreement. But the two governments did not seem able to get together.
I do not think it is fair to blame the province of New Brunswick. In all fairness I feel that the fault lay in a lack of policy because from my own experience in the house I believe that many members who supported the government of the day were sympathetic and felt that something should be done. As a matter of fact I have talked with them. Of course it may be the case that a government cannot always put something like this into operation unless it feels it has a sound reason for advancing it. No government had ever been in power so long without having a policy and I suppose the government of the day felt it could not establish a policy for New Brunswick.
On behalf of the people of my constituency and my province I want to say again that we appreciate the fact that the new government has given early recognition to our need. I do not think the government is going to go overboard and give us everything we want, but to me this is the first stepping stone in the development of a policy which will not only help us but will help other provinces as well. I hope that members of the house will support the legislation and I feel that they will.

maintopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOAN OF $30 MILLION TO PROVINCE OF NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the resolution is very clear and simple. It will have two effects; first, to reduce the interest obligations of the provincial government of New Brunswick and, second, because of that reduction to reduce the cost of the generation of electricity by the Beechwood project. As the hon. member who has just taken his seat pointed out, during previous sessions a desire has been expressed by members from the Atlantic provinces for policies which would result in the development of cheaper electricity in that area, and we did have a response to that last spring in the budget of Mr. Harris. However, the resolution to follow the present one will provide a better opportunity to compare that proposal and the proposal that will be under discussion.
I find it rather difficult to approach a discussion of the resolution now before us because an examination of the economic

merits of Beechwood cannot lead to anything but futility on the part of the House of Commons inasmuch as we are asked to examine the merits of a project which is now completed and in operation. The House of Commons is asked to share retroactively in the responsibility for a decision taken in 1955 by the government of New Brunswick. At this moment some years later we are asked to share in that responsibility and to approve, as it were, without an opportunity to have any real effect on the decision then made. We have been presented today, Mr. Chairman, with a number of arguments that might have changed that decision if the House of Commons had had the opportunity to pass judgment on them.
For example, the hon. member for Charlotte pointed out that the proper development of Beechwood might and apparently does involve co-operation with the United States and the province of Quebec, and if that is the case then the House of Commons at the time of the origin of the project might have had an opportunity to deal with that matter. We are asked to deal with an omelet that is now presented to us.
However, while that is true it is not the main source of difficulty for me. This resolution having to do with the development of hydro power in the province of New Brunswick is followed on the order paper by another resolution dealing with the development of thermal power in the Atlantic provinces as a whole. One block of electricity is to be developed through hydro power and another block of electricity in the same region is to be developed through the use of coal.
The presentation of these two companion resolutions reveals to me the inconsistent attitude which the government is taking toward the coal industry in the Atlantic provinces. The hon. member who just took his seat asked members of the house to support this resolution and certainly I have given some consideration as to whether I should support the resolution because of the effect which this development will have upon future markets for coal in the province of Nova Scotia.
I am, of course, sympathetic to the development of New Brunswick in any shape or form but I am also conscious of the responsibility which I, as a member from Nova Scotia, have to promote those matters that are of assistance to the coal industry. I should like to know from the Minister of Finance or from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources how many tons of coal would be used annually.

This was a project which the government of the day could very easily have turned its back on, through lack of support, by the then federal government, but it did not do so; it took the bull by the horns and started out on its own. New Brunswick is indeed fortunate that they have the potential hydro development available. We in Nova Scotia have depleted a large part of our hydro resources and those remaining are receiving active consideration at the present time. We have in Nova Scotia, however, millions of tons of coal which will in the near future, and under a resolution to be introduced here in parliament later today, supply our province with thermal power, our mines with markets, and our people with an ambition that has lain dormant for a great many years.

speechtext:
I should like to take a moment to define again, if I may, what I consider is really relevant. We are being asked, as the Minister of Finance has admitted, to approve a bill to carry out stage 1 of the national development policy initiated in the speech from the throne. This stage 1 is entirely within the confines of one of the ten provinces. Two hundred and fifty-five of the members of this house represent the other nine provinces. We are being asked -and I take no exception to this-to vote a considerable sum of money,-by way of loan, it is true,-for this project. It seems to me that we are entitled to be told what up to now is the whole policy of the government which is to take the place of what the Prime Minister, before he was Prime Minister, referred to as the negative, haphazard one of the previous administration.
Nothing in the speech from the throne, or nothing that we have been told in the seven months in which this government has been in office, has disclosed any project whatever that was new or any suggestion of any project that was new. We have this Beechwood project which has been discussed for the last seven or eight years and which, as the Prime Minister said when he congratulated the premier of New Brunswick, had been completed some time ago. We are being asked


to do what I would call refunding of the money spent on this project. The Minister of Finance quarrels with my language. He does so, I presume, because he does not want to admit that it is just as reasonable for the government of Nova Scotia to ask for the refunding of the loan for something they did a year or two ago as it is to ask for the immediate refunding of this one.
The effect of this loan will be to reduce the cost of power in New Brunswick to some degree. The minister himself admitted that. Why should we be asked to do that in New Brunswick and why should it be refused in Nova Scotia merely because the government of Nova Scotia more prudently arranged for a bond issue? Surely what the Minister of Finance has enunciated, if I understood him correctly, is that if a province goes ahead and does something imprudently and then finds it cannot float a bond issue itself, it is then our duty to do it for them; but if they are prudent and careful, as Nova Scotia was, and do it themselves, then they are not entitled to as favourable treatment. Is that the policy? It seems to me that what we have had so far are a few bits and pieces left over from before June 10 and that we should not be asked on this basis to approve this resolution without being told what else the government is going to do in this field.
I am particularly interested, of course, in knowing what the government intends to do about the province of Newfoundland. We are undoubtedly in more need of electrical development there than is any other part of Canada. There is no other province where there are more homes, in proportion to the total, without electricity. I do not think even the Minister of Finance would contend that the province of Newfoundland is in a better financial position to float a loan to develop electricity or indeed to reduce the cost of electricity that is already developed, because that is all we are doing here. We are not developing anything new; it is all completed. The Minister of Finance says it is in operation. We are simply reducing the cost of something that is already in operation. Why should not that be done in Newfoundland merely because bonds have been floated. It seems to me that is a very difficult principle to get anyone to accept. Why should it not be done in Nova Scotia? What is going to be done for Prince Edward Island? I understand that earlier today the Prime Minister told the house that he had had a telegram only yesterday from the premier of Prince Edward Island-
