Mr. Chairman, when we rose for the dinner recess I was just pointing out to the committee that the minister had made it clear that the purpose of the bill to be founded on the resolution was to refund the moneys expended by the government of New Brunswick on the Beechwood project. I know that the minister does not agree with the definition of the word "refund" that is found in all standard dictionaries and that I am using here, but the minister has indicated that this project by that time will have been completed, that there will be no new work, that there will be no further employment in building the project.
In other words, it is not something new that is being done. It is a project on which the work is entirely completed, a project that is in operation and on which there is a debt which the federal government intends to assume, if the bill is passed, up to $30 million. That is what this proposition is. We are being asked to agree with the government that it is expedient to lend the government of New Brunswick up to $30 million to refund these obligations of the government of New Brunswick for this particular project in this particular place, a project which the minister has told us is part of the national development policy of the government.
We have the Prime Minister's answer in the house to a question I put on the order
Beechwood Power Project Loan paper which was obviously very definitely considered, that this is not an isolated matter, that it is part of a policy that is applicable in all the provinces or in any province -I want to be quite accurate-in which there are comparable conditions. It seems to me it is quite impossible for us to decide in the knowledge of all the circumstances whether it is really expedient to make this very considerable charge upon the taxpayers of Canada for a project, however meritorious it may be, and I am not discussing its merit at the moment, in one particular place in one particular province, until we know how this policy which the government has told us is a national policy applicable across Canada is to be applied in other provinces, and what in the opinion of the government would constitute the similar circumstances to which the Prime Minister referred.
It does seem to me, sir, that it is very hard for a member representing a constituency in the province of Newfoundland, where the need for the development of power is as great as it is in that province, to say that it is the right thing to do to vote public moneys for this project in another province unless we can be satisfied that Canadian citizens living in another province, a province with even less resources, will be similarly treated by the government in like circumstances. I must say, sir, that it is impossible for me to understand how the government can make any kind of valid distinction making any sense at all between lending this money to New Brunswick to pay off the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Bank of Commerce or whatever chartered bank it may be and saying on the other hand that it would be quite improper to lend money, say, to the government of Nova Scotia to pay off a bond issue, thus reducing the cost of power to the users in Nova Scotia. It does not seem to me that we should be asked to adopt a policy of limited application to a very limited area of the country unless we know that if comparable circumstances exist it will be applied in other places as well.
I must say I was rather astonished by the answer given by the Prime Minister to the third question I put to him and which he answered on November 22. That question was:
Are such loans available only for projects owned by provincial governments or provincial crown agencies or will they be available to private power companies sponsored by a provincial government?
This is the answer given by this great Tory government, the apostles of free enterprise. It would not have surprised me in the least bit if a government headed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, or by his

Beechwood. Power Project Loan colleague, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, if there ever were such a government in this country, would have given this kind of answer but it does surprise me that such an answer should be given by this Tory government that boasted during the election campaign that they were going to take government out of business, that they were going to restore free enterprise. What did they say? The answer given was no, such loans would not be available to private companies.

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the government of Canada to enter into agreements with any of the Atlantic provinces to provide assistance in the generation of electric energy by thermal electric power projects and in the control and transmission of electric energy, and including provisions for the payment of a subvention on coal used in the production of electric energy.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on December 21, 1957 this house agreed to a motion made by myself that it consider this resolution, which had been recommended
Atlantic Provinces Power Development by His Excellency. The measure which it is proposed to introduce entails financial consequences which will greatly benefit the Atlantic provinces.
As announced in this house on November 14, 1957, by the Prime Minister, apart from the financing of Beechwood, which is being dealt with separately, the present proposed measure would do two things. For those Atlantic provinces who desire such aid the dominion government would build for and sell to the provinces such thermal plants and transmission facilities as may be agreed upon. The second part of the program would consist of granting a subvention on Atlantic provinces' coal consumed for the production of power in the Atlantic provinces. This subvention would be so calculated as to eliminate, so far as possible, the differential in price between coal used in the Atlantic area and coal used in Ontario for the production of power.
We have had from the provinces their estimates of the cost of the construction programs for the fiscal years 1957-58 and 1958-59. For Nova Scotia the program would amount to about $3.4 million, and for New Brunswick it would amount to about $9.3 million, or a grand total of about $12.7 million for those two years. To complete the immediate program thus embarked upon would cost possibly another $3.5 million for Nova Scotia and another $8.5 million for New Brunswick, or a total of about $12 million. Thus the projects presently planned would cost about $25 million.
There will undoubtedly be other programs submitted in future years which will require to be considered by parliament. These cannot be known at this stage, and will depend upon the extent and pace of development in the Atlantic area, and also on whether provinces in that area other than New Brunswick and Nova Scotia wish to take advantage of the program. Hon. members would like to have a forecast of what the program might cost, say over the course of the next ten years.
We have, at present, no program of development put before this government by the governments of Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. As far as the other two Atlantic provinces are concerned, there might be as many guesses as there are experts on the subject of power. One group of experts who have looked at the question recently, Montreal Engineering Company Limited, estimated that an interconnected program within and between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick might give a total installed capacity of 507 megawatts by 1967 at a capital escalated cost of about $105 million. This would provide
3038	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development for two plants in New Brunswick, eight in Nova Scotia and the requisite transmission and terminal facilities. This, Mr. Chairman,' is only one estimate of an order of magnitude.
For the purposes of the two fiscal years now in contemplation, a total of $12.7 million for construction of plants and transmission lines will certainly be required. Appropriate items will be included in the further supplementary estimates for 1957-58 and in the estimates for 1958-59. Hon. members of the committee will wish to note, Mr. Chairman, that the amounts of money expended on the construction program will all be refunded with interest so that this phase of the program is a self-liquidating one.
The second phase of the government's program will consist of a subvention on the Atlantic provinces' coal used for the production of thermal electric energy in the Atlantic provinces. For the purpose of this resolution the annual cost of such a subvention is currently estimated to amount to $1.7 million. It will, of course, vary with the amount of coal actually used for power purposes. This sum of money will not be recovered directly. But it is the conviction of this government that the industry promoted and generated by this subvention to the provision of cheaper electric energy in the Atlantic provinces will be worth many times the money expended. Given electric energy at a cost competitive with that available in other areas of Canada the people of the Atlantic region will be in a much better position to compete successfully with all comers in Canada or elsewhere.
Perhaps I should make it clear, Mr. Chairman, that the legislation to be introduced under the terms of this resolution will not in itself appropriate or authorize the expenditure of any sums of money. The legislation is enabling legislation, to permit agreements to be entered into for the program I have outlined. The funds required each year to carry out the program for that year will be sought from parliament in the normal fashion in the estimates. It is the purpose of this government through this and the Beechwood measure to enable the people of the Atlantic provinces to have cheaper electric energy. It will then be possible for them to develop, process and utilize more effectively their natural resources. It will make for a better Canada. It is the first step in what I hope will be a continuing series of measures designed to develop Canada. As agreements in principle are reached with other provinces on projects the pattern of the government's over-all policy for development will become clear.
This program is a co-operative one with the provinces in the Atlantic area. Some hon.
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1

members may say that there is nothing in it for Newfoundland or Prince Edward Island That, Mr. Chairman, is not an accurate statement. True, it may be inappropriate for Newfoundland at this time to seek to build thermal plants. However, transmission lines and related facilities, which are, as you know, often very costly-and indeed of great importance in the development of a power system-could be built by the federal government and sold to Newfoundland on the same basis as for Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. The same can be done for Prince Edward Island.
This program of lending aid to provinces which have not shared the advantages of the remainder of Canada in the development of their natural resources will help not only to develop Canada's natural resources in that area, but such a program is among the first steps of this government to speed up the development of Canada's natural resources by Canadians for Canadians.
However important and essential it is, firstly, to obtain thermal power generating and transmission facilities in the Atlantic provinces and, secondly, to obtain them on these advantageous financial terms, the resolution forecasts yet another means of reducing the cost of thermal power in the Atlantic provinces. And it is this means which alone is truly significant in the reduction of the mill rate to the power user. I refer to the subvention on Atlantic provinces' coal consumed in the manufacture of thermal power in these provinces if the provinces so request.
As hon. members know, the coal used in different plants most often has differing heat value. The coal subvention contemplated by this bill will be calculated at that rate per million heat units-technically known as British thermal units

necessary to equalize the cost of the heat in the coal produced and used in the Atlantic thermal plants with the same cost in central Canada thermal plants.
The final and exact figure of the subvention will form part of the agreements to be entered into with the respective provinces. Reports received from 12 plants in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick show that in the 12 months ending August 31, 1957 these plants used 927,257 tons at a total cost of $9,150,580 or an average cost of $9.69 per ton. This coal contained, on the average, 11,885 British thermal units per pound. The average cost per million B.T.U. was 41.51 cents. The central Canada plants consumed during the same period 1,459,881 tons of coal and the cost per million B.T.U. was 34.73 cents. On the basis of these figures, the assistance would be the difference between 41.51 cents and 34.73 cents or 6.78 cents per million B.T.U.

The rate of assistance per ton will vary with the quality of the coal used in the individual plants. For example, a plant using coal with a heat value of 13,325 B.T.U. per pound would qualify for $1.81 per ton at the rate of 6.78 cents per million B.T.U., while another plant using coal of 11,190 B.T.U. per pound would rate $1.62.
After discussion with the premiers of the two provinces which have sought federal aid so far it has been agreed that the assistance will be at a defined rate for a period of five years from the date of the agreement. May I say at this point, Mr. Chairman, how much I appreciated the friendly and co-operative spirit of Premiers Flemming and Stanfield in the meeting I had with them. They most ably represented the interests of their provinces, but when a compromise had to be reached they agreed co-operatively and in a sense of complete understanding.
I should add, Mr. Chairman, that the subvention will not be restricted to thermal plants operated by power utilities or commissions but would also be paid to industrial plants producing thermal power for their own use and for sale. The subvention would be paid to the province's designated agency and the province will be responsible for a fair distribution among power producers.
The subvention on coal for power production based on such a differential and paid on performance should, firstly, give the Atlantic provinces an opportunity of competing more successfully with the rest of Canada from the viewpoint of power costs. Secondly, there will be an indirect support for Atlantic seaboard coal to be used in this region. And, thirdly, there will be an incentive to buy, produce and deliver coal of good quality for the production of the cheapest power possible in the Atlantic region. As I have indicated previously, the cost of the coal subvention for a full year is estimated to be $1,700,000. Such a subvention would be paid from funds appropriated annually for this purpose by parliament.
Hon. members will recall from my statement that the program of work envisaged for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick over the fiscal years of 1957-58 and 1958-59 is of the order of $12.7 million. In the case of Nova Scotia, one 20 megawatt addition will be made to the Trenton thermal plant at a total cost of about $3.2 million. In the two fiscal years mentioned the cost for the Trenton plant would be about $2.3 million. Transmission lines in Nova Scotia and terminal facilities would account for another $1 million.
So far as New Brunswick is concerned, a 50 megawatt plant will be established at East
Atlantic Provinces Power Development Saint John. In the two fiscal years, the cost will amount to about $3.3 million. The ultimate cost of this plant is estimated to be $10 million. Transmission lines and facilities would cost another $6 million in the two fiscal years.
At the end of these two fiscal years the two provinces will be well on their way not only to complete interconnections within the provinces but between both these provinces. This should relieve both these provinces of the necessity of providing immediately for additional reserve or standby capacity as a linked-up system will provide its own reserve capacity and two linked-up systems will provide mutual support to each other.
On the previous resolution, the treasury benches were asked questions about comparative power figures and the Minister of Finance assured hon. members that I would give these during the course of my remarks this evening. The government was asked, what would be the cost of replacing Beech-wood power by thermal power, assuming 300 million kilowatt hours, 6 per cent money and a coal subvention. I should state here that the answer given was that such Beech-wood power would cost between 7 and 7.5 mills. That was the answer I gave earlier in the house and which now appears in Hansard.
It has been estimated that 300 million kilowatt hours produced by a 50 megawatt unit at Saint John financed at 6 per cent would cost about 8.93 mills per kilowatt hour. The coal subvention on such an amount of power, I am informed, would come to about .9 of a mill and thus, in this case, the net cost of replacement power would be about 8 mills compared with 7 to 7.5 mills in the case of hydro power from Beechwood. Therefore, hydro power, even with a subvention on coal at Saint John, is definitely cheaper.

The New Brunswick and Nova Scotia systems we speak about are to be integrated systems. The Beechwood project will not be used to carry the base load. I heard a good deal of discussion about this this afternoon and I should like to say a word or two about it.
The base load will be carried by thermal power. I am not a power systems engineer, Mr. Chairman, but I am informed that the cost of power is determined largely by what it will cost to meet the peak demand. With two excellent units such as at the new Beechwood plant the cost of peaking will be below that of thermal power. Moreover, further thermal plants will not be needed to meet the peak demands which are growing at a very rapid rate in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
The best engineering advice has indicated that the two Beechwood units now being installed can be "used to good advantage for supplying peak power and secondary energy". The same engineering advice recommends the construction of a 50 megawatt unit in east Saint John if immediate interconnection is not available. This same advice recommends interconnections between the two provinces. This is the program we propose to follow which, I feel convinced, will result in a lowering of costs for industrial power and the further development of the natural resources of these Atlantic provinces.
I have spoken tonight on the resolution, Mr. Chairman, and I think that hon. members will realize that in dealing with the problem of a power system in the four Atlantic provinces a good deal of the information can only be brought out properly in the committee stage. But in view of the turn that the debate on the Beechwood resolution took today I want to conclude with one or two observations which I think will bear listening to.
In the first place, when we looked at this problem in the maritimes we were faced with the fact that here was an area in Canada short of power and generally speaking what power they had in these two provinces in particular was very high-cost power. Then we had to take a look at the situation not only from the point of view of handling the power requirements of these two provinces but of fitting them into the over-all national development philosophy.

I want to go back to the second part of my observations. The Atlantic provinces are a power deficit area, an area which presented tremendous economic difficulties in working out the thermal power grid problem. We recognized that every device possible had to be used to achieve the aim of the government which was to provide cheaper power in this area. The devices used were first of all the usual device of interconnections. Second, there was the use of a coal subvention. Third, there was the question of tying in the hydro power in the plants already existing in the two provinces with the basic thermal plants to give maximum efficiency.
May I give hon. members one figure which I think will be useful in this debate. If we had kept the two provinces separate we would have had to build 16 plants while this integrated system only calls for 10 plants. By the combination of the thermal and hydro plants in one province together with the combination of such plants between the two provinces we were able to cut the cost little by little until I think we have reached the objective that was so necessary to attract industry to the Atlantic provinces at a figure approaching 7 mills.
I thought that when I came to the house with this information there would be general

support among all parties and I felt very proud indeed that as a new member of the house I should be allowed to play a part in one of the moves that will help one part of Canada to achieve some measure of economic uplift that has been so badly needed.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources said that he was proud to outline this program for the building of thermal plants and
transmission lines in the Atlantic provinces.
I am proud that he feels proud, because after all he was just dealing with the implementation of Liberal policy which was announced in this house by Mr. Harris in his budget speech on March 14 last. I, myself on April 9 gave more details about the project which was being developed by the previous administration to build thermal power plants and transmission lines for interconnection purposes in the Atlantic provinces. The statement I made at the time was a comprehensive one and an outline of the plans we had in mind can be found at page 3293 and following of Hansard for last session. The object of the then government was to secure power at the lowest possible cost, and at the same time use maritime coal as the fuel for that purpose. I said at that time, and may I quote from page 3294 of Hansard for April 9, 1957:
It has been decided that an immediate study should be undertaken to determine what new capacity may be required in the two provinces-*
That is in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
-and, having regard to possible new interconnection lines, what would be the most effective and economic location. This study will be undertaken by Montreal Engineering Company as consultants for the Northern Canada Power Commission. The study will be carried out in full consultation with the power commissions of the two provinces.
The report of the Montreal Engineering Company was expected in the month of August. In the meantime there was correspondence between the authorities in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and myself. There were meetings of the officials of the two provinces and of the department to settle all possible details and be ready to proceed at once when the report of the Montreal Engineering Company was received. When the present government took over we had made good progress in our discussions with the provinces.
According to the correspondence which has been tabled in this house, negotiations between my immediate successor, now the Minister of Agriculture, and Mr. Flemming, the premier of New Brunswick, continued in July. In the first days of August the report of the Montreal Engineering Company was received by the government and copies were sent to the premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The report has now been tabled in this house. This report contains very definite recommendations. On November 14, when he tabled the report, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources had this to say, and I quote from page 1102 of Hansard for the present session:
In doing so-

I ask this question in the light of the comments made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources which I quoted a few moments ago, comments made in this house on November 14. I ask the question also in the light of the comment made on the report in a letter dated September 6 last and written by Mr. R. E. Tweeddale, chief engineer of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, to the premier of New Brunswick.
In the correspondence which was tabled in this house, according to an order of the house on a motion by the hon. member for Gloucester, there is a copy of a letter written by the premier of New Brunswick on October 11 to the Prime Minister, enclosing a copy of his comments on a memorandum of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources dated September 30 and entitled "Power Problem in the Atlantic Provinces". Alvin Hamilton". I am sorry I am giving his name, sir, but this is the title of the paper to which I am referring.
There are four pages of these comments and at one point, on page 3, it is said that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National

I should like to know what has been done about the criticisms of the premier of New Brunswick to try to satisfy him. These criticisms are contained in those comments I was mentioning, and they can be found at pages 95 and following of sessional paper No. 117. Mr. Chairman, I think we are all pretty well agreed that these measures serve to implement Conservative policy and Liberal promises. I recall very well during the last campaign picking up the Liberal manifesto of the 1949 election when these very resolutions which we are introducing here tonight were the crux and the basis of the Liberal campaign at that time. It has always been the task of a Conservative government to implement Liberal promises and I feel quite certain that our sincere friends

on the other side of the house will not hesitate to give this measure the support it deserves.

All that is needed is a review of our demands over the years and the do-nothing reaction these demands received from the former government to understand very clearly the record of the late Liberal party as being one of indifference, inaction and downright irresponsibility toward the people of the maritime provinces.
In the long and colourful history of the maritime provinces the rights of those provinces have stood out as being neglected by the federal government. I think we must recognize that our economic troubles in the maritime provinces really began with confederation. The promises and the considerations upon which the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-

3046	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Provinces Power Development thermo electric projects, and also in the control and transmission of electric energy together with provisions for the payment of subventions on coal used in the production of electric energy. In the correspondence and documents tabled under Sessional Paper 117-B we had access to the correspondence which took place since the announcement made by the former minister of finance in presenting his budget on March 14, 1957. Included in this sessional paper was a letter from the premier of New Brunswick to the Prime Minister of Canada, under date of October 11, 1957, which read as follows:
My dear Prime Minister:
I am enclosing a copy of my comments on the memorandum of Hon. Alvin Hamilton, dated September 30, in connection with "Power Problem in Atlantic Provinces", which, I trust, will be helpful to you in presenting our point of view.

Also attached to this letter was a memorandum from the premier of New Brunswick on the proposals of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources relating to financial assistance with power development in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Yesterday, rising on a question of privilege, I asked the minister for the tabling of this proposal which was not included in the sessional paper, and I stated rightly that it was part of the documents which were asked for following a return to an address of the House of Commons, dated November 6, 1957, for a copy of all correspondence and other documents exchanged between the federal government or any of its departments and the governments of the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia or their respective power commissions, from April 1, 1957 to date, regarding the development of electrical energy.

A copy was shown to the premier of the province of New Brunswick. My department advises me that they did not consider it as part of their records and since it was not used in the department, it is not part of the documents requested.

Without having seen the federal proposal, if we are to judge from the memorandum showing the reaction of the premier of New Brunswick we must conclude that the

unqualified acceptance of the proposal would entail specific points of difficulty in the conclusion of any agreement. For instance, in his reply the premier of New Brunswick stated that the method of financing power development outlined in the proposal entailed rates of interest considerably in excess of anything proposed to date by the government of Canada to the government of New Brunswick.
It is further stated that if the rate of interest for power development should be substantially above the federal long term rate, and if the price of power from new generating units financed with federal assistance was to be based on the principle of earning 5 to 6 per cent on invested capital, as stated in the memorandum which has been refused to us for obvious reasons, then the price of power would be at a level which would completely discourage development by high load factor power users in the pulp and paper industry and in the metallurgical industry.
It is clearly stated that the memorandum does not conform to the principles which have been discussed over the last six months by representatives of the government of Canada and representatives of the governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and which were dealt with in detail at the meeting held in Ottawa on August 13 and 14 between the Prime Minister of Canada and certain of his officials, and the premiers of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and certain of their officials.
In its report of the power supply of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia for the Northern Canada Power Commission, the Montreal Engineering Company made certain recommendations which I think should be placed on the record:
(1)	That the additional power that will be required in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in the next decade be generated in the main in a number of large steam plants feeding into an interprovineial grid. Any hydro power that can be obtained to better advantage should also be developed.
(2)	That the steam plants be located where they will be reasonably close to the load centres, have rail connections with the Sydney and Pictou coal fields, and be on tidewater, so that coal and oil can be purchased in the cheapest markets.
(3)	That the sites for such steam plants be Saint John, Halifax, Trenton and Sydney, and possibly given sufficient increase in load in northeastern New Brunswick, near Chatham or Bathurst.
(4)	That the electric utilities endeavour to complete the interconnections between their power systems by the end of 1959, the transmission lines to be single circuit and operated initially at 138 KV. As regards the new sections of line that will complete the link between Saint John and Halifax, serious consideration should be given to designing them so that they can eventually be operated at 230 KV.
(5)	That the utilities also do their best to work out an agreement between them that will provide
Atlantic Provinces Power Development for the orderly installation of additional generating capacity and for the sharing of the cost of spare capacity.
(6)	That if an adequate interconnection cannot be arranged in the near future, the 50 megawatt unit now on order by the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission be installed in Saint John with all possible dispatch.
(7)	That if the completion of an adequate interconnection between the New Brunswick and Nova Scotia power systems can be assured, and if no unforseen increase in load develops, the installation of the first unit in the new steam plant in Saint John be deferred until 1961, and if cancellation and other charges are not excessive, consideration be given to increasing its capacity substantially.
It appears obvious that in view of this recommendation, and judging from what has been said so far, the government has decided to proceed with the installation of large steam plants feeding into an interprovineial grid. At this point, I want to urge the government to give very serious consideration to the location of the plants to be built in the next year or so in order to provide the necessary power for the development of our mining resources. The Brunswick Mining and Smelting Corporation have already announced their decision to proceed with the construction of a lead and zinc mill and also with a lead smelter at Caron Point, near Bathurst. The Prime Minister on September 27 last, made the announcement that the government was prepared to share in a major harbour development at Bathurst in conjunction with the mining company's plans for a $20 million expansion and development program in that area. Such a project if realized would have automatically required a substantial output of electrical energy and it would only have been logical, practical and economical that such thermo plants be constructed at Caron Point at the proximity of the load centre required by this proposed mineral expansion. Furthermore, Caron Point would have offered year-round deep-water facilities in addition to its rail connection which could make it an ideal site for such a proposed unit.
When the increase in load will be required in eastern New Brunswick it will naturally originate from the development of our mineral deposits and I was hoping that the government would be practical in choosing the Caron Point site for its first thermo plant, thereby taking advantage of relatively cheap transportation, the most advantageous in the province for the coal or oil required for the operation of the plant. Unfortunately, the announcement made in the last few weeks by the Brunswick Mining and Smelting Company to the effect that their operations would be curtailed for a certain period has greatly upset the people in Gloucester county and

Business of the House the entire population of New Brunswick. I understand the officials of this company were in Ottawa during the week of December 15 and that discussions took place at that time.

speechtext:
1.	Is the Post Office Department making reductions in the staff at the Regina post office now or in the immediate future?
2.	If so, in what branches or categories of service have, or are these reductions to be made?
3.	What is the reason for the reduction, or proposed reduction, in each instance?
4.	On whose advice or recommendation was the decision made?
5.	What provision is being made for employees affected by present or proposed staff reductions?
Answer by: Hon. W. M. Hamilton (Postmaster
General):
1.	The strength of the staffs at all larger post offices is under constant review and, when warranted, additions or reductions are made. At present the staff of part-time employees at Regina is under study but no decisions have yet been made.
2.	See answer to No. 1.
3.	See answer to No. 1.
4.	Decisions are usually based on the recommendations of senior field officers.
5.	Employees affected by staff reductions are assigned, where possible, to existing vacancies.
